content:
Many common beliefs about arthritis are wrong, and some stop people getting help. Arthritis is not just an old person's condition, exercise does not wear joints out, and there is a lot that can be done to reduce pain. Here we check ten common myths against NHS and NICE guidance.

Myth 1: Arthritis is just part of getting old

Fact: Osteoarthritis does become more common with age, but it is not inevitable, and many older people never develop painful arthritis. Other types, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis, often start in young or middle-aged adults. Children can get arthritis too. Joint pain at any age deserves proper assessment.

Myth 2: Exercise will wear out my joints

Fact: The opposite is true. NICE (NG226) recommends exercise as a core treatment for osteoarthritis. Moving joints helps keep cartilage healthy, and stronger muscles take load off painful joints. Some aching when you start is normal and does not mean you are causing damage. Start gently and build up.

Myth 3: Rest is the best treatment

Fact: Short rest during a bad flare can help, but long periods of rest make joints stiffer and muscles weaker, which tends to increase pain. Pacing, meaning a steady amount of activity each day, works better than lots of rest followed by bursts of activity.

Myth 4: Cracking your knuckles causes arthritis

Fact: There is no good evidence that knuckle cracking causes arthritis. The sound comes from gas bubbles in the joint fluid. Painless clicking is very common and usually harmless. Clicking with pain, swelling or locking should be checked.

Myth 5: Nothing can be done about arthritis

Fact: There is no cure for most types, but there is a great deal that helps. Exercise, weight management, physiotherapy, pain relief, aids and adaptations and, if needed, joint replacement all help osteoarthritis. For inflammatory arthritis, disease-modifying medicines and biologics can control the condition and prevent damage, and many people reach remission.

Myth 6: Diet can cure arthritis

Fact: No diet cures arthritis. A healthy, balanced diet supports overall health, and losing weight if you are overweight reduces strain on hips and knees. In gout, cutting down on alcohol, sugary drinks and some foods can help reduce attacks. Be wary of products or plans that promise to cure arthritis, and check supplements with your pharmacist, as some interact with medicines.

Myth 7: Arthritis only affects joints

Fact: Inflammatory types can affect the whole body. Rheumatoid arthritis can cause fatigue and affect the lungs, eyes and heart. Lupus can affect skin, kidneys and blood. Even osteoarthritis can affect sleep, mood and work. Good care looks at the whole person.

Myth 8: The weather causes arthritis

Fact: Weather does not cause arthritis. Some people notice their joints feel worse in cold or damp weather, and that experience is real. Keeping warm and active can help. Moving to a sunnier place will not cure arthritis.

Myth 9: If my X-ray looks bad, I must be in a lot of pain

Fact: X-ray changes and pain often do not match. Some people have major changes on X-ray with little pain, and others have severe pain with mild changes. NICE says osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed without an X-ray. Treatment is guided by your symptoms and how they affect your life, not just a scan.

Myth 10: Joint replacement is the only real answer

Fact: Surgery helps many people with severe hip or knee osteoarthritis, but most people manage well without it. NICE recommends trying exercise, weight management and other non-surgical treatments first. Surgery is considered when symptoms seriously affect quality of life despite these.

Myth 11: Young people do not get arthritis

Fact: Children and young people can develop juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and inflammatory arthritis often starts in people in their twenties and thirties. Sports injuries can also lead to osteoarthritis earlier in life.

Why the myths matter

Believing these myths can lead people to stop moving, delay seeing a doctor or spend money on treatments that do not work. If you are unsure about something you have heard, ask your GP, pharmacist or physiotherapist. Reliable sources include the NHS website and NICE guidance.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
